title: Lawmakers ask FAA to pause use of new AI tool in DC-area flight management
source_used: Reuters text as carried by CNA (full text). The Reuters page returned HTTP 401.
key_facts: More than two dozen lawmakers asked the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) on 13 Oct 2026 to pause a new AI tool that helps air traffic controllers in the Washington area, citing safety concerns.
Signers include Democratic Representatives Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Don Beyer and Senator Chris Van Hollen.
Their letter says they have seen no safety evaluation and testing reports, nor any effort to train aviation safety personnel on using the tool, and seeks an answer by 19 Oct.
The FAA began using the software last month; it uses predictive analytics to improve how flights are managed.

In June the FAA awarded Air Space Intelligence an $875 million, 12-year contract for the system, called SMART, which analyses schedules, weather, airport capacity and airspace conditions to predict traffic flows and spot conflicts.
The FAA uses it first around Washington, D.C. and plans to expand it gradually to other parts of the country.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy called it essentially "dumb AI" and said controllers remain in charge; the Department of Transportation says it uses over 200 data streams and produces scheduling recommendations but does not actively manage planes.
FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford told Reuters earlier it is "going to be transformational".
quote_evidence: More than two dozen lawmakers asked the Federal Aviation Administration to pause the use of a new AI tool in the Washington area to assist air traffic controllers, citing safety concerns.
"Air traffic control leaves zero margin for error," Ocasio-Cortez said Tuesday, calling for the pause.

"Air traffic controllers will always control the airspace. This is just giving additional tools for controllers to better manage" weather and other issues," Duffy said on Fox Business’ "Big Money in the Morning."
why_it_matters_hint: Lawmakers say an AI tool already in use around Washington's airports has not been shown to be safe, while officials say it only advises controllers.
notes: Reuters story read on CNA's copy because the Reuters page was blocked (HTTP 401); the text carries Reuters' dateline and photo credits.
